I'm sure this has some major gaps because I'm new to doing substantive edits like this to HTML, but I've marked this as ready for review because I'm interested in feedback at this point.

Also cc:ing @emilio and @bkardell as folks who may be interested generally or in the particular open issue that I've raised above.
I'm not sure whether the `positive` position in mozilla/standards-positions#831 counts as implementer interest for the purpose of a WHATWG PR.
Yeah it does, feel free to update OP accordingly.

This looks ready to merge. I'll be OOO until July 11, but would be happy to merge then if @dbaron is.

Some things to maybe work on in the meantime:

- Do you think you have test coverage for all the cases listed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/9400#discussion_r1231851118 ?
- Do we have any further thoughts (e.g., asking the OpenUI community members) on the exclusivity while disconnected? I'm particularly wondering if they might be surprised by `details.open` having non-exclusive behavior during the "preparation phase" where they're setting up their DOM nodes before insertion.

FYI, two other bits of feedback (in addition to the above) that I'm currently tracking:
* FreedomScientific/standards-support#725 reports an issue with Chrome + JAWS, apparently on the JAWS side, regarding use of the `name` attribute on all elements (including those that don't "have" a `name` attribute) for computation of the accessible name.  It's not entirely clear to me how serious this is (which includes how likely it is to get fixed in JAWS and how quickly such a fix would reach users).
* I don't yet understand the feedback starting in https://github.com/mozilla/standards-positions/issues/831#issuecomment-1616678969 (and I think previously in a comment thread in this PR) but my initial reaction to it does make me think that perhaps I should be adding a *document* conformance requirement that, in a document that uses the `name` attribute on `details` elements, at most one of the elements in a given name group should have an `open` attribute.

I just made one additional edit in an attempt to address the feedback starting in https://github.com/mozilla/standards-positions/issues/831#issuecomment-1616678969 .  I'm not sure whether or not it satisfies the concern there; however, I think the change I've made is desirable even if it doesn't.  This change adds a pair of author conformance requirements and a note explaining them.  (I'm not really sure if I need two separate requirements to cover (1) the static state of a document that a validator would check, and (2) the result of script modifications; I'm certainly open to better ways to word the requirement.)

So this additional edit could probably use some amount of review.

I see nothing in here about providing an accessible name / grouping context for the accordion. I may also be missing it because it is called something else and I am looking for the wrong words.

I used the following example at the informal poll on GitHub (https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/812#issuecomment-1692360733). A non-ARIA-powered native HTML implementation can lean on group role and/or landmark semantics, which already exist in browsers and are exposed via Accessibility APIs. Essentially converting the following construct into a dedicated HTML element:

```html
<section role="group" aria-labelledby="accName">
  <details>[…]</details>
  <details>[…]</details>
  <details>[…]</details>
</section>
```

My concern is that screen reader users will otherwise have no context that these disparate details/summary widgets are related and may not understand why their content in other details/summary widgets keeps going away. At the very least a grouping context (and name) can be a cue.

It can have the side benefit of minimizing the extra content that developers will stuff between details/summary widgets -- which is something requested in the poll and which poses a genuine 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence or 2.4.3 Focus Order WCAG violation risk.

@aardrian Are you essentially suggesting something like an `<accordion>` element that would contain the related `<details>` elements, either in addition to or instead of linking them with a `name` attribute?

At at first glance, it seems like it would be caused by the build trying to use a wattsi version which thinks the `ref` element is void element. But the current version of wattsi knows it’s not void. @dbaron I believe the cause of the build problem should now be fixed in this PR branch. Please pull and try. Note that I squashed the changes into a single commit and force-pushed it to the PR branch.

With the squashed version, the build is fixed for me -- thanks for fixing that.

> Note that I squashed the changes into a single commit and force-pushed it to the PR branch.

It looks like the squashed version is exactly the same as the previous version, at least according to `git diff 93deda9b3e6675c5cb012d159a4237f3353aeb1f..53e7ef42a14038c5e862eded503f17c44915129e`.  Is whether wattsi builds correctly or not really a function of the git history?

I _think_ `git diff` intentionally skips over merge commit-caused differences. Using a non-git-based diff tool against the raw files in those cases might be revealing. (Or I might be misremembering how `git diff` works.)

> I _think_ `git diff` intentionally skips over merge commit-caused differences.

Yeah

> Using a non-git-based diff tool against the raw files in those cases might be revealing.

You can also see it from the GitHub UI, if you look at the merge commit itself — in this case, https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/93deda9b3e6675c5cb012d159a4237f3353aeb1f

…which shows the merge commit also included a change to `review-drafts/2023-07.wattsi`.

And from the command line, you can take the hashes for the parent commits (9b76787 and d6ce12a) — also shown in the GitHub UI at https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/93deda9b3e6675c5cb012d159a4237f3353aeb1f, in the `2 parents 9b76787 + d6ce12a commit 93deda9 patch diff` line — and you can do this:

```
git diff --name-only 9b767879...d6ce12a4
```
…which outputs:
```
review-drafts/2023-07.wattsi
source
```

I still think it looks like the merge commit itself is fine.  The change to `review-drafts/2023-07.wattsi` is a change relative to the first parent of the merge (the old version of the branch) but not relative to the second (the updates to `main`).  The `git` command line UI has special UI for showing merge commits (showing only parts updated relative to both parents, with double-diff UI) whereas the github UI seems to show the merge relative only to the first parent.  (I should perhaps have done the merge so as to cause the first parent and second parent to be the other way around, but I don't do git merges often enough to remember the correct way, or for that matter to know if there's a standard git convention for which parent of a merge should be first or second, but I suppose the "normal" merge direction is to merge a feature branch into main rather than the other way around.)

I think the problem is that `html-build/build.sh` executes `CHANGED_FILES=$(git --git-dir="$HTML_GIT_DIR" diff --name-only HEAD^ HEAD)` (which assumes that only the most recent commit is relevant -- meaning that if I add another commit to the branch things will start working again) as part of figuring out if review drafts need to be processed.  This means that it will break on the merge commit, but should be fixed again if I commit something else on top of the merge commit.
I pushed a new merge that had the first parent and second parent the other way around (i.e., probably the correct way around), which also fixes the problem because `HEAD^` refers to the first parent.
I've now added changes to implement https://github.com/openui/open-ui/issues/786#issuecomment-1710709737 .

@dbaron 
> Are you essentially suggesting something like an `<accordion>` element that would contain the related `<details>` elements, either in addition to or instead of linking them with a name attribute?

Missed this, sorry for late response.

I am not suggesting a new element yet. Perhaps a rule that when all `<details>` with a `name` attribute are preceded by a heading and in the same container with no non-`<details>` elements between them, that the heading becomes the group name. Or require a `<section>` wrapper that has an accName (heading). Or sure, a new `<accordion>` element.

If there is a wrapper, the `name` attribute could be mooted.

I don't want to require being *siblings* within the same container, because developers do sometimes have real reasons to want extra container elements around things (as much as we'd like to avoid having to add such elements).  So I think it's entirely reasonable for the linked elements to be first cousins, or even second or third cousins... but I think I agree that it's desirable to not have substantive content between them.  (Although I do wonder if there are some cases where it would be desirable, that I'm not thinking of...)

I'll try to think about how to word such a statement in the spec.

@aardrian In 65a26ed I think I've addressed a part of your concern, although probably not all of it.

I think some of what you were suggesting may belong in html-aam rather than html: in particular, if we're going to give advice about inferring an accessible name for a section from its header for this particular case.  (At least, unless that's already an existing rule for a more general case?)

I think it's possible HTML could say a little bit more, but I do want to (a) avoid giving advice that I wouldn't stand by 100% or very nearly 100% of the time and (b) avoid giving advice that's prematurely assuming what html-aam is going to say.

Does that seem reasonable?  Is there other particular advice you think HTML could give now?  And do you think it makes sense to open an html-aam issue on the topic?

Hey, I am very late to this discussion (and my first time entering a discussion like this so if there are better ways to ask, please let me know.). Also apologies if this has been answered and I missed it, but how will the grouping be exposed to assistive tech? At the moment the pattern most prefer for an exclusive accordion is: ```html

FAQs (for example)

Accordion 1
Accordion 1
``` However if there is a `name` attribute added to make an exclusive accordion, will this be exposed as a group of items in some way in the accessibility tree / to assistive tech (AT)? As if that is the case that could lead to a lot of duplication of "group" announcements (compounded by `` itself being announced as a group like "Summary, group" in some screen reader / browser combos.). If it is announced as a group, how would you label such a group? If it isn't announced as a group, is there some way a screen reader user (for example) will know other elements have been collapsed when they open another? (minor point as this is an existing problem, which is why most prefer the `role="group"` attribute to be added to at least show the controls are related), or is this down to the developer to follow the pattern I described earlier / how we currently do this? I did check the updated HTML spec, but I am not sure if I missed this point. Thanks in advance and love this addition by the way!
